newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-No win on aboriginal and immigration policy.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-No win on aboriginal and immigration policy.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Tuesday identified the basic political dynamic operating in aboriginal and immigration policy: it's a no-win area for the new government.
The news media, urged on by some lobby groups, suspects that the Liberal-Nationals do not have the former Labor government's commitment to the interests of aborigines and immigrants.
The Labor opposition, therefore, is highly sensitive to the slightest sign from the government confirming this suspicion.
In effect, there is almost nothing that the government can do to change the former government's policy without Labor implying in a receptive news media that the conservatives are racists.
Could the government cut the annual immigration target for economic reasons without Labor implying that it did not like immigrants? Probably not.

Howard said in parliamentary question time on Tuesday: "We are not going to cop a situation where just because we do things differently, every time we announce a change in policy that gives a rhetorical license to those on the other side of this parliament, and others in the community, to brand us as insensitive or racist."
Well, they may have to cop that situation, because there is no sign that it is going to change.
Effectively, the government has two choices:
-- It can leave both areas alone, as far as it can bear to.
-- Or it can battle on with changes and hope that the criticims fade away, encouraged by complaints of political correctness.
But notice that Howard could probably help his own cause by being a little more extravagant in his support for aboriginal and immigration affairs.
No doubt he is being thoroughly honest when he says he is concerned about these issues. But such comments sound like motherhood statements: everyone says that these days.
Instead, a loud and abusive condemnation of politically incorrect independent Pauline Hanson would be just the ticket.
Perhaps the problem is that, as opinion polls show, too many Australians have little disagreement with Hanson.
